title: Command-line tools with Core.Command
body: `Command` builds command-line programs from typed parameters. A flag such as `flag "-n" (optional_with_default 3 int) ~doc:"N ..."` knows its type, its default and its help text, and `anon ("TEXT" %: string)` declares a positional argument. You get argument parsing, error messages and `-help` output without writing any of that yourself.

The parameters are combined applicatively with `let%map_open.Command n = ... and text = ... in fun () -> ...`. The result is a `unit -> unit` action that runs only after every argument has parsed successfully, which keeps parsing and behaviour separate. `Command_unix.run` (from `core_unix.command_unix`) turns the command into a program.

Keep the real work in a library and make the executable a thin shell. The library function `Wordfreq.top ~n text` is then testable without spawning a process, and the executable only wires parsed arguments to it.
challenge: Implement `Wordfreq.top ~n text` in src/wordfreq.ml: split on whitespace, lower-case, count words, sort by count descending then word ascending, and keep the first n. The CLI in bin/main.ml is already wired up.
projectInstructions: Build with `dune build --root .`, then run `dune exec --root . bin/main.exe -- -n 2 "a b a c a b"`. Try `-help` too. Edit only src/wordfreq.ml.
question: Why keep the counting logic in a library instead of in the executable?
correct: A library function can be tested directly, while the executable only wires parsed arguments to it
reasoning: Separating parsing from behaviour makes the behaviour reusable and testable without a process boundary.
